paper.title: Systematic and dynamic task coding in the frontal cortex
paper.abstract: Behavioral flexibility depends on the capacity to form and utilize task representations. Prior work has shown that baseline activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) can differ between two tasks. Comparing more than two tasks makes it possible to ask whether different neuronal populations share a common form of task encoding, that is, a conserved representational geometry across tasks. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform 6 cognitive tasks and recorded spiking activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons in the frontal eye field (FEF) or the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), one area per session. During the fixation period, before any task-specific stimulus appeared, the population activity state already reflected the upcoming task, and task identity could be decoded on single trials. Strikingly, the geometry of the 6 task states was conserved across populations recorded in different sessions, across the two areas, and across the two monkeys. Global signals that differ between tasks, such as expected reward, task difficulty, and attention, measured by reward amount, hit rate, and reaction time, did not fully account for this shared geometry. These findings suggest that the frontal cortex systematically adjusts its population state to encode and prepare for the upcoming task.

paper.title: Dynamical mean-field theory of latching Potts networks
paper.abstract: Spontaneous transitions between memories, as observed in internally generated cognition such as mind-wandering and free association, require neural dynamics capable of destabilizing one attractive memory state and moving towards another. We ask what minimal representational structure is required for such transitions to emerge in random associative networks. To address this question, we study Potts associative networks with $S$ active states per unit and slow adaptive thresholds. The $S=1$ case can model a standard Hopfield-like network of binary units. We employ dynamical mean-field theory in the extensive-load regime, where the number of stored patterns scales linearly with network size and connectivity, and we focus on transitions between two condensed memories, which are singled out in the connectivity matrix. In the finite-load regime, we show that transitions are governed by an effective drive term, whose sign and temporal evolution distinguish high-latching (structured), low-latching (random), and non-latching regimes. The resulting phase diagram shows that adaptation alone is not sufficient: transitions only occur within certain ranges of the overlap between the two memories. In the binary case $S=1$, in particular, no unit can be active in both memories but in different Potts states, thus strongly supressing the high-latching, structured transitions that exist for $S>1$. In the extensive-load regime, non-condensed memories generate colored fluctuations and retarded self-interactions through an effective memory kernel. We find that latching trajectories change the effective timescale of this kernel, a dynamical signature of transitions in the extensive-load regime. These results indicate that multi-state Potts-like representations are essential for structured memory-to-memory transitions, a hallmark of spontaneous thought.
